content: Good evening. Sorry for the late message — it's been one of those Sundays where I finally sit down at nine o'clock and realize I haven't eaten a proper meal since Thursday. But I wanted to catch up while things are still fresh. We had a strong close to the week, and I have a lot on my mind about where we are heading into the back half of Q1.

No need to apologize — Sunday evenings are often the only time a restaurant owner gets to think without someone needing something from them immediately. Take your time. You mentioned a strong close to the week and a lot on your mind about the back half of Q1. Why don't you start wherever feels most pressing? Is it the financial picture, the team situation, or something on the operations side?

Honestly, it's all of them at once, but let me start with the team because that's the thing I'm most relieved about. Marco Petrelli is back. He returned March 1 from his vacation in Modena, and I cannot overstate how much of a difference that makes in the kitchen. The sous chef Hiroshi did a genuinely good job holding things together during the two weeks Marco was away, but the energy is different when Marco is running the pass. Service times are tighter, the brigade communicates better, and the food tastes the way it's supposed to taste. I noticed it immediately on the first night of service after he came back.

That's a real relief to hear. Two weeks without your head chef is a significant test for any kitchen, and it sounds like Hiroshi held the line well — which is worth acknowledging separately. But the rhythm a kitchen builds around its lead cook is hard to replicate, and it makes sense that the whole operation snapped back into shape once Marco was at the pass again. Did he come back energized from the trip, or does it usually take him a few days to readjust to the pace of service in Tokyo after being in Emilia-Romagna?

He came back extremely energized. More than I expected, honestly. Modena does something to him every time he visits — he reconnects with the food at a very fundamental level, and that always translates into new ideas once he's back here. But this trip was different because he didn't just come back with ideas. He came back with a direct business contact. He spent time with a family he knows from his years working in the region, and through them he connected with Acetaia Giusti. You might know the name — they're one of the oldest balsamic producers in Modena, operating since 1605. Marco now has a direct line to them for supply, which means we can potentially bypass the importer we've been using for our balsamic. We've been running some numbers this week, and the preliminary estimate is an 18% savings vs current import costs if we go direct through Petrelli's contact.

Acetaia Giusti is exactly the kind of name that means something on a menu — one of the oldest producers in Modena, genuine DOP pedigree, and a story guests can connect to. But beyond the prestige angle, an 18% savings vs current import costs is not a small number, especially on a product like aged balsamic where the per-liter cost is significant. A few things worth thinking through before you formalize the arrangement: First, what are the minimum order quantities Acetaia Giusti requires for direct supply? The savings only hold if you can move the volume without accumulating stock that ties up working capital or risks quality degradation. Second, how does the logistics chain look? Direct import from a Modenese producer means you're now handling customs clearance, cold-chain verification, and delivery timing yourself rather than leaning on the importer's infrastructure. Third — and this is more of a due diligence point — does Marco have a written understanding with his contact, or is this still at the handshake stage? You'll want something on paper before you start depending on this channel for a core ingredient. None of these are reasons not to pursue it. They're the practical questions that turn a promising lead into a reliable supply relationship.

Those are exactly the right questions and I'm glad you raised them. On the MOQ point: Marco says the contact has indicated we can start with smaller shipments while we establish the relationship, so that's not an immediate constraint. The logistics piece is the bigger open question — our current importer handles all the paperwork and we've never dealt with direct import from Italy at this scale. I'm going to reach out to the freight forwarder our sake supplier uses and get a realistic picture of what that process looks like. On the written understanding: it's still at the handshake stage right now, which is why I haven't told anyone outside the management team. I want to see what comes out of the next conversation Marco has with them before I start planning around it. But I'm optimistic. He also brought back some artisanal balsamic from the family contact directly — not Acetaia Giusti product, just something the family produces privately for their own use and as gifts — and Marco used it in a special dish on Friday and Saturday. Guests loved it. It created a natural conversation starter about what we're working on with the supply side.

The way you introduced that balsamic — through a special, letting the product speak for itself, giving guests a story to engage with — is exactly right. You didn't overpromise anything about the new supply relationship, and now there's genuine guest anticipation around whatever comes next from that direction. That's a valuable asset whether or not the Acetaia Giusti arrangement closes the way you're hoping.

The freight forwarder consultation is the right move. Your sake supplier's contact will have practical experience with Japanese customs for imported food products, and they'll be able to tell you quickly whether direct import is operationally viable at your current volume or whether you'd be better served finding a smaller specialty importer who can consolidate your Italian dry goods. The 18% savings is real, but the question is always: savings on what annualized spend, and does the operational overhead eat into that margin? If your current annual balsamic spend through the importer is, say, 800,000 yen, then 18% is about 144,000 yen — meaningful, but not enough to justify a complex new logistics arrangement on its own. If you're spending more heavily than that on the product, the math shifts.

On the broader Q1 picture — you said you had a lot on your mind there. What does the financial situation look like heading into the close of the quarter?

That's actually what I want to talk about next because it's the thing keeping me up. The Q1 revenue total is 11.8 million yen versus plan of 12.5 million. We are 700,000 yen short of where we expected to be at this point, and there are only a few weeks left in the quarter. I knew January was going to be soft — it always is, and we planned for a slow first two weeks — but February ran softer than I modeled. We had three large reservation groups cancel in the second half of February, two of them within 48 hours of the reservation date. That's a scenario I didn't build into the model, and it hurt us.

That gap between 11.8 million yen and 12.5 million is uncomfortable, but it's also a story with a clear cause, which matters a great deal when you're figuring out what to do about it. You're not looking at a structural problem — you're looking at a concentration risk that materialized in February: a small number of large-group cancellations, two of them within 48 hours, with no time to fill the covers. That's a revenue protection issue, not a demand issue.

A few things worth separating out here. First, do you have a cancellation policy for large group reservations that includes a deposit or a per-cover fee for late cancellations? If not, this episode is strong justification for implementing one. Two within-48-hour cancellations on large groups is exactly the scenario that a deposit policy is designed to either prevent or partially compensate. Second, how are you tracking the shortfall against the rest of March? You have a few weeks left in the quarter. Is there a realistic scenario where you close some of that 700,000 yen gap, or are you already forecasting that Q1 closes below plan and managing expectations accordingly? Third — and this connects to what comes next — does the shortfall change your thinking at all on the revenue levers you have available, like the pricing review you mentioned at some point, or the wine club trajectory?

All three of those threads are exactly where I was headed. On the deposit policy: we have a policy for groups of eight or more, but not below that threshold. One of the February cancellations was a group of six, which slipped under it. I'm going to close that gap. The new policy will apply to groups of five or more with a 48-hour cancellation window for a full refund, and a 50% per-cover charge for cancellations inside that window. I drafted it this week and I'll put it in place for reservations starting from next month.

On the March outlook: I'm not counting on closing the full gap. I think we'll end Q1 somewhere in the 12 to 12.2 million range if March continues at the pace we've been running. That's still below plan, but I'd rather be honest with myself about that now than scramble and do something disruptive to the guest experience just to chase a number.

And on the revenue levers — yes, the wine club and the pricing question are both live conversations for me right now.

The policy change is the right call and it's well-designed. Five or more with a 48-hour window gives you protection without being onerous for the average guest or small party. The 50% per-cover charge inside the window is industry-standard for fine dining at your level, and guests who book large tables at an osteria in Higashi-Azabu understand that their reservation has real cost implications for the kitchen. You'll occasionally get pushback, but it will be rare, and the policy's existence will change booking behavior in your favor more often than you'll have to enforce it.

On the Q1 close: projecting 12 to 12.2 million and holding to it rather than chasing 12.5 is the right discipline. The scramble scenario — flash promotions, rushed group outreach, discounting — almost always costs more in brand equity than the revenue it recovers. You're running a restaurant where the guest experience and the positioning are the primary assets. Protect those even when the quarter doesn't close the way you planned.

Let's talk about the wine club and the pricing question, then. Which one is more time-sensitive for you right now?

The wine club is more time-sensitive because I have a hard target and a deadline. Cantina Morishita — that's what we named it — currently has 23 members signed, and my target is 40 by April. I set that number because 40 members at the current membership fee structure generates enough recurring revenue to cover a meaningful portion of our wine procurement costs, which are the single largest variable line item after labor. At 23 members, I'm just over halfway there, and I have roughly six weeks to close the remaining 17 spots. The mechanics are in place — the welcome packet is ready, the first quarterly member event is scheduled for April 12th — so this is purely an outreach and conversion problem now.

Twenty-three members signed for Cantina Morishita with a target of 40 by April is actually a reasonably strong position to be in, even though it doesn't feel that way when you're staring at a 17-spot gap. Think about the math on your side: you built this club, presumably with no prior infrastructure, and you got 23 people to commit. That tells you the proposition works. The question now is purely one of reach — you've converted the people who were already in your orbit, and the next 17 need a slightly longer path to find you.

A few channels worth thinking about specifically for the next six weeks. First, every current member is a warm referral source. People who join something like Cantina Morishita — a wine club at a restaurant they already love — tend to have friends with similar tastes and spending profiles. A structured referral offer, even something simple like a complimentary bottle of wine for any referral who converts, gives them a reason to actively recruit rather than just mention it in passing. The conversion cost is low and the trust transfer from an existing member is high.

Second, the April 12th event is an asset you can use as a prospecting tool right now. Consider inviting eight to ten non-members — people who've dined with you multiple times, guests who've shown interest in your wine list, good corporate diners — to attend as guests of the club. They experience the evening alongside paying members, see the format, taste the wine, and have a natural conversion moment at the end. Done well, that one event could close six or eight of the remaining spots.

Third — and this is more granular — what's the breakdown of your 23 current members by channel? Did most of them come from in-restaurant conversations, from social media, from a launch email, or from something else? The answer tells you a lot about where to concentrate the next six weeks of outreach.

The breakdown is roughly what you'd expect: about 16 of the 23 came from direct in-restaurant conversations, either I spoke to them at the table or Marco mentioned it during service when the timing felt right. The other seven came from the announcement email I sent to the full reservation list in mid-February. I haven't done any social media push yet because I wanted to have the structure properly in place before I opened it up more widely. The referral idea is interesting — I hadn't framed it that way, but you're right that the members we have are exactly the kind of people who know other people like themselves. And the prospect-guest idea for the April 12th event is something I'm going to think hard about. I was treating the first event as purely for signed members, but opening six or eight seats to high-potential prospects changes the dynamic of the evening in a useful way. I want to be careful about the ratio so it doesn't feel like a sales event to the paying members, but a small number of guests wouldn't disrupt that.

The social media angle is something I've been avoiding partly out of caution and partly because I'm not sure what the right tone is for Cantina Morishita on Instagram. The membership fee is not inexpensive, and I don't want to come across as pushing a luxury product in a way that feels off-brand for how we've always communicated.

Your instinct about the ratio on the April 12th event is exactly right. Six guests against seventeen or so paying members keeps the event feeling like what it's supposed to be — a gathering for the club — while still giving you meaningful prospect exposure. The guests feel like they're being brought into something exclusive rather than pitched to, which is the right emotional register. You might position the invitation to those guests as something like: 'We're hosting the inaugural Cantina Morishita evening on April 12th and would love to have you join us as our guest for the evening.' No mention of membership, no sales context. Let the evening do the work. The conversation about joining happens afterward, naturally.

On the Instagram question: I think the caution is well-placed, but the constraint you've identified — 'how do I talk about something premium without sounding like I'm pushing a luxury product' — actually has a clean solution for a restaurant like yours. You don't talk about the membership. You talk about the wine. Show the bottles Marco and you are tasting for the next event. Share a photo from a producer visit. Write a short caption about why you chose a particular Barolo for the April menu. The content isn't an advertisement for Cantina Morishita; it's an expression of the point of view that makes Cantina Morishita worth joining. People who are interested will ask. That keeps the tone consistent with how you've always communicated while building organic interest in the club.

Now — you mentioned the pricing review. That feels like it's been sitting in the background of this whole conversation. What's the situation there?

The pricing conversation is the one I've been most hesitant to have, even with myself. But the Q1 picture and the cost environment we're operating in — ingredient costs are up, the yen is still not where I'd like it to be for imports, and energy costs haven't come down the way I hoped — all of that is pointing in the same direction. I'm looking at raising prices on 4 menu items. Not across the board, which I think would be a mistake, but on four specific dishes where I believe the current pricing genuinely underrepresents the value we're delivering and where the ingredient cost basis has shifted enough to make the current price feel like it's working against us. I haven't decided which four yet. Marco and I are going to sit down Tuesday to go through the full menu cost analysis. But I wanted to think through the strategic frame before I go into that conversation with him.

The instinct to do targeted increases rather than an across-the-board adjustment is correct for a restaurant at your positioning. A blanket price revision sends a signal to your regular guests that the restaurant's economics are under pressure, and it invites comparison with every other item on the menu. Selective increases — done thoughtfully and on dishes where the rationale is defensible — can go almost unnoticed if the changes land on the right items.

For the Tuesday conversation with Marco, here is a frame that tends to produce better decisions than starting from cost analysis alone. Think about the menu in three buckets. The first bucket is dishes where the gap between perceived guest value and current price is largest — these are the dishes guests order enthusiastically, remark on, and sometimes specifically mention in reviews or when they come back. These are your safest candidates for a price increase, because the guest's value reference point already sits above what you're charging. The second bucket is dishes where ingredient cost has moved significantly but the dish is a staple — something guests order so reliably that changing the price creates visible friction. These need to be treated carefully; sometimes a portion or presentation adjustment buys you more than a price change. The third bucket is dishes that are underperforming on both margin and order frequency. These are candidates for reformulation or removal, not price increases.

When you identify the 4 menu items for the increase, a few principles tend to hold across restaurants at your level. Price changes that round to a clean number are less psychologically jarring than odd increments — a dish moving from 2,800 yen to 3,200 yen reads differently than one moving to 3,050 yen. Changes in the 10% to 15% range are typically absorbed without guest comment; anything above 20% on a well-known dish benefits from a narrative — a new preparation, a sourcing story, something that gives the guest a reason to feel the change is justified. And timing matters: introducing new prices alongside a seasonal menu update or a new offering provides natural cover and makes the change feel like part of an evolution rather than a correction.

Given that you're already thinking about the Acetaia Giusti balsamic relationship, and Marco came back from Modena with energy and new ideas — there may be a natural moment here to tie a small menu evolution to both the pricing review and the story you want to tell about the kitchen's direction. That's not a reason to manufacture changes that don't make sense on their own, but if the timing aligns, it's worth considering.

That three-bucket framework is useful and I'm going to use it on Tuesday. I think I already have a rough intuition about which dishes fall into which bucket, but going through the cost sheets with Marco with that structure in mind will sharpen the conversation. The point about tying the price review to the seasonal update and the new sourcing story is also well taken. We do a spring menu refresh in late March, which is actually perfectly timed. If we finalize the 4 menu items for the increase and introduce them as part of the spring menu announcement, it lands as a natural evolution. And if the Acetaia Giusti relationship advances the way I'm hoping, there's a story to tell alongside it about where the kitchen is going. I'm feeling better about how this all fits together than I did two hours ago. Let me ask you one more thing before I actually eat something: what's the most important thing for me to track between now and the end of Q1 to make sure I'm not surprised by anything?

Three things, and they're all closely connected to the conversations we just had.

First, watch the Cantina Morishita conversion rate weekly, not monthly. You have six weeks to close 17 spots, which means you need roughly three new members per week on average. That's not a difficult pace, but it's easy to let two or three weeks slip by without meaningful outreach and then face a gap that's hard to close. Set a simple weekly check: how many new members signed this week, what were the touchpoints that generated them, and what specific outreach is scheduled for the next seven days. The referral structure and the prospect-guest strategy for April 12th are the two highest-leverage moves, so those deserve explicit calendar time, not just good intentions.

Second, track the March reservation mix more actively than you usually would. You identified that the February shortfall came from large-group cancellations that you couldn't have predicted individually, but you can now look at your March bookings and identify which nights carry meaningful concentration risk — single large tables or group reservations that account for a disproportionate share of that evening's expected revenue. On those specific nights, watch for cancellation signals and have a contingency in mind, even if it's just a standby list of regulars you can call. You probably won't need it, but knowing you have it changes how you feel going into those evenings.

Third, and most practically: before the Tuesday conversation with Marco, pull the cost sheet for every dish you're considering and calculate what the current contribution margin looks like at the present price and what it would look like at a 10% and 15% increase. Go into that conversation with the numbers already in front of you. Marco will have strong opinions about the food and the guest experience — which is exactly what you want — but the financial decisions need to come from you, informed by real margin data. If you walk in with that analysis done, the conversation will be much sharper and you'll be less likely to leave decisions open that should be closed on Tuesday.

Eat something. The quarter is recoverable, the team is back in shape, and you have more levers to pull than you did at the start of this conversation.
